passage: In the statistics tutorial at her Toronto college, Soo-ah had noticed Leila right away: sharp questions in week one, then silence. By week five, Leila pushed the worksheet away before reading it. "I'm just not a numbers person. I'll fail anyway." Soo-ah had seen her midterm: one early slip had cost her badly, but the reasoning was good. So instead of the full worksheet, Soo-ah slid across a single question, one Leila could solve with what she already knew. "Only this one. Five minutes." Leila sighed and did it. Right. Soo-ah gave her another, slightly harder. Right again. By the end of the hour Leila had done four and was frowning at the fifth by choice. Soo-ah said nothing about it, only ticked the page.

qa.q: What did Leila say when she pushed the worksheet away?
qa.a: "I'm just not a numbers person. I'll fail anyway."

qa.q: Why might Leila have given up before even reading the worksheet?
qa.a: The bad midterm made her believe effort was useless, so not trying felt safer than failing again.

qa.q: Which choice by Soo-ah worked, and why?
qa.a: Giving one question Leila could solve, then slightly harder ones; each success chipped away at the belief that effort changes nothing.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah feel as Leila frowns at the fifth question by choice?
qa.a: Soo-ah is probably quietly pleased and hopeful, seeing the small steps work, but says nothing so the choice stays Leila's own.

grounding: In a college tutorial, Soo-ah sees a capable student give up in advance and gives her small tasks she can succeed at, which rebuilds effort.

passage: At the polytechnic workshop, Preeti ma'am watched Vijay stand at his bench with his arms folded while the others started on the circuit board. "Why aren't you starting?" "No point, ma'am. Mine never works. Last three boards, all failed." Preeti knew his theory marks were among the best in the class. She also knew how the last three boards had gone: one bad solder each time, and laughter from the next bench when the last one smoked. So she took away the full board and handed him a small strip. "Just solder these four joints. Nothing else." He did it, grumbling. She tested them: perfect. "Now these four." Also perfect. By the end of the session he'd finished the whole power section, and he was the one asking for the next task.

qa.q: What did Preeti ma'am hand Vijay instead of the full board?
qa.a: A small strip, with four joints to solder.

qa.q: Why did Vijay stand with his arms folded instead of starting?
qa.a: Vijay felt discouraged and embarrassed: three failed boards and the laughter had convinced him his work would fail again, so starting seemed pointless.

qa.q: Which choice by Preeti ma'am changed the session?
qa.a: Replacing the whole board with four joints he could get right, then building up, so success came before doubt could stop him.

qa.q: How might the classmates who laughed see Vijay by the end of the session?
qa.a: They may be surprised to see him finish the whole power section and ask for more, seeing him as capable rather than as the one whose board smoked.

grounding: An instructor sees a capable student refuse to start after repeated failures and assigns small, winnable steps.

passage:
Dear Ujjwal,
I noticed something in class on Monday and wanted to write rather than mention it in front of everyone. When I handed out the essay prompt, you wrote "I can't write essays" at the top of the page and put your pen down. You've said this before. But I've read your lab reports, and they are clear and well argued. So here's my suggestion for this week: don't write the essay. Write only the first paragraph, the one that says what you think and why, and bring it to my office on Thursday. That's all. One paragraph is something I know you can manage. If it goes the way I expect, we'll add the second next week.
Best,
Parveen Qureshi
Lecturer, English Communication

qa.q: What did Ujjwal write at the top of the essay prompt?
qa.a: "I can't write essays."

qa.q: What might Ujjwal be feeling when the pen goes down?
qa.a: Ujjwal likely feels defeated in advance, sure that effort on an essay will fail again, so stopping feels safer than trying.

qa.q: What choice does Parveen make, and why might it work?
qa.a: Asking for just one paragraph, a task Ujjwal can succeed at, so a real success can start to break the belief that effort is useless.

qa.q: How might Parveen Qureshi feel while waiting for the paragraph on Thursday?
qa.a: Parveen seems hopeful and confident in Ujjwal, having read the clear lab reports and expecting the one paragraph to go well.

grounding: A lecturer notices a capable student give up before starting and writes to set one small, achievable task.

passage: It's small, the thing I'm proudest of this year. I'm Reena, I teach anatomy at a nursing college in Kozhikode, and in the first term I had a student called Yusuf. Clever, quick, the best questions in week one. By week four he'd look at a test paper and write "I can't do this" across the top before reading a single question. His first mark had been poor, and he'd decided that was who he was. So I stopped handing him full tests. I gave him one diagram of the hand bones, just ten labels. He got nine. The next week, a diagram of the foot. Then one short answer. By March he sat the whole paper. He didn't top it. But he didn't write "can't" either.

qa.q: What did Reena give Yusuf instead of a full test?
qa.a: One diagram of the hand bones, just ten labels.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf write 'I can't do this' before reading a question?
qa.a: After one poor mark he decided failing was who he was, so trying seemed pointless and giving up first protected him from another disappointment.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it work?
qa.a: Getting nine of ten labels on a small diagram; small successes, built up week by week, gave Yusuf evidence that his effort did count.

qa.q: What was it like for Reena to watch a capable student give up?
qa.a: Reena clearly noticed the gap between his sharp early questions and the 'can't', and seems more determined than annoyed, choosing small tasks over lectures.

grounding: A teacher sees a capable student declare defeat before starting and gives small tasks he can succeed at, slowly changing his belief.

passage: I'm Payal, and I teach accounts at an evening college in Nagpur. Vandana, nineteen, works in a pharmacy by day and comes to my class at six. In the first week she solved a ledger problem faster than anyone. After she failed the first unit test, something shut. Now when I hand out problems, she pushes the sheet an inch away and says, "Ma'am, I'm not an accounts person. No use." I can't know everything she's carrying. But last Tuesday I skipped the worksheet for her and gave her just one entry: record a cash sale of five hundred rupees. She hesitated, wrote it, and looked up. "That's it?" "That's it. Correct." On Thursday I gave her three. Today she asked for the worksheet herself.

qa.q: What single entry did Payal give Vandana?
qa.a: Record a cash sale of five hundred rupees.

qa.q: What does Vandana's 'That's it?' suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Surprise and a flicker of relief; after expecting to fail, getting one task right challenged her belief that effort was no use.

qa.q: What choice did Payal make, and why did it work better than pushing the full worksheet?
qa.a: She gave Vandana one small entry, then three; small wins built evidence that trying works, until Vandana asked for the worksheet herself.

qa.q: How might Vandana see Payal's approach?
qa.a: Vandana may feel that Payal hasn't given up on her and isn't forcing her either, which makes it safer to try again.

grounding: A teacher sees a capable student give up before starting and gives one small task she can do, then a few more.
